description: We're Kepler-16, a small team of three tackling the SPHEREx challenge with real NASA data. Between us we cover Python, web development and design, and we love making science fun and accessible for everyone. Our team is complete, so we're not recruiting new members, but we're always happy to connect with other teams. Good luck to everyone this year!
summary: In 1930, Pluto was found by flipping between two photos of the night sky: every star stayed still, and one dot moved. SKY BLINK gives that discovery power to everyone. It is a free website that turns real images from NASA's SPHEREx telescope into something anyone can explore, by sight or by sound. Search a star, and SKY BLINK blinks SPHEREx images taken months apart. It marks whatever moved or changed brightness and reveals the object's infrared fingerprint from 0.75 to 5 µm, and every view can also be heard, with spoken descriptions. This is exactly how SPHEREx's repeated all-sky maps can expose a hidden Planet X. In real data, our Planet X Hunter shows Pluto moving 5 arcminutes in 17 days while the stars stay still. We tested all five challenge targets honestly, finding methane in Epsilon Indi B and RW Aurigae brightening by about 21%. SPHEREx data sits in scientific archives few people can use. SKY BLINK opens it to students, teachers, and blind and low-vision explorers, in English and Bahasa Melayu, because space is for everyone.
details:
SKY BLINK: See it. Hear it. Find it.

Welcome screen: SKY BLINK — explore the sky by sight or by sound.

In 1930, Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto by flipping between two photographs of the night sky. Every star stayed still; one tiny dot jumped. Today NASA's SPHEREx telescope photographs the entire sky in 102 colours of infrared light every six months, so that same discovery trick now works across the whole sky. But the data sits in scientific archives most people, especially students and people who cannot see, will never open. SKY BLINK changes that: a free website that turns real SPHEREx images into something anyone can explore, by sight or by sound.

Home page: "See how the sky changes — by sight or by sound." A real SPHEREx blink of interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS moving over 8.2 hours, with quick links to Search, Planet X Hunter and Listen.

What it does and how it works

1. Search the sky

The Search page: type a name or coordinates, or tap a challenge target to open a real saved search.

Type a star name or coordinates. SKY BLINK gathers SPHEREx images of that spot from NASA/IPAC IRSA, lines them up north-up, adds the images of each visit together, and plays the visits like a short video. A change finder marks anything that moved or changed brightness. ESA Gaia DR3 and NASA AllWISE overlays show which objects are already known. The website includes real saved searches for all 5 challenge targets plus Luhman 16; searching any new position runs through our Python helper (code on GitHub).

Search result: brown dwarf Epsilon Indi B in real SPHEREx images, with Gaia star circles and its motion of 4.69″ per year.

Search result: young star RW Aurigae, about 21% brighter in Feb 2026 than in Sep 2025.

Live search proof: Luhman 16, the third-closest star system to the Sun, searched straight from NASA’s archive with our Python helper.

Spectrum fingerprint (inside Search).

Epsilon Indi B’s infrared fingerprint from 32 SPHEREx images: dark at the methane band, the sign of a cold brown dwarf.

For any searched target, SKY BLINK measures every SPHEREx image at the exact infrared colour where the target landed, building a 0.75–5 µm spectrum. Water and methane bands are marked; the cold brown dwarfs Epsilon Indi B and Luhman 16 show the methane dip.

2. Planet X Hunter.

Planet X Hunter: Pluto drifting across real SPHEREx images while the stars stay still.

Real SPHEREx images of Pluto and Makemake (positions from NASA JPL Horizons) show a far-away world drifting while the stars stay still: Pluto moves 5 arcminutes in 17 days. A distance calculator shows that even at 500 times Earth’s distance from the Sun, a hidden Planet X would still drift about 8 SPHEREx pixels in a week.

3. Listen mode.

Listen mode for blind and low-vision users: learn the sounds, follow the comet by ear, and try the Sonar challenge.

Every view can be heard: left–right position becomes stereo, height becomes pitch, brightness becomes loudness, and spoken descriptions guide the listener. A Sonar challenge lets users find a comet by ear.

4. Learn and play.

Spot it: find the moving object in two blinking real images, the way Pluto was discovered.

Case study part 1: interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS moving across 10 real SPHEREx images, with its path and known asteroids.

Case study part 2: the comet's infrared fingerprint; carbon dioxide glows brightest, much stronger in December 2025 after it passed the Sun.

One-minute lessons in English and Bahasa Melayu.

A classroom quiz with a 40-minute lesson plan.

Results on the challenge targets (real SPHEREx data)

Benefits and intended impact

•         Opens real NASA SPHEREx data to students, teachers and the public with no installation and no login.

•         Includes blind and low-vision people through sound and speech, not as an afterthought but in every view.

•         Teaches the real method astronomers use to find moving worlds, and lets anyone practise it on real data.

•         Ready for classrooms: bilingual lessons, a quiz and a lesson plan.

Tools and languages

Python (astropy, astroquery, numpy, scipy, reproject, Pillow) for the data pipeline and live search helper; HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the website; Web Audio API and the browser speech feature for sound; GitHub Pages for hosting. Code: https://github.com/debwex/skyblink

What makes it creative

SKY BLINK turns a scientific archive into something you can watch, hear and play. Sound is not an add-on: every image, motion and spectrum has a sound version. And Planet X Hunter turns Pluto's discovery into hands-on practice for finding a planet nobody has seen yet.

Factors we considered

•         Accessibility: sound, speech, keyboard control and a phone-friendly layout.

•         Honesty: we show limits as well as successes (faint and saturated targets, candidates that must be checked by blinking).

•         Accuracy: positions corrected for each star's motion through space, problem pixels masked, and all data credited.

•         Safety and rules: no images or voices of team members; all AI use disclosed.

Behind the Scenes

How SKY BLINK works: our Python pipeline from the NASA archive to sight and sound, with an honest list of its limits.

SKY BLINK on a phone: no app, no login, works on any device.
